messages.subject: defining post-stratification cluster size categories
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

=20

Just a quick question about post-stratification by cluster size. Is
there an easy way to combine clusters into larger categories (i.e.
cluster sizes of between 1 and 4 into a single strata: '1-4') within

messages.subject: Re: defining post-stratification cluster size categories
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark, list,

If you want to stratify all components of estimation (detection function,
encounter rate, cluster size) by cluster size group, then you could either
do this by

- Post stratifying by cluster size group, as you indicate.  In this case
you'll need a new field that defines the groupings, in the observation
layer.  An example of this is the "Cluster strat" field in the Stratify
example sample project.

- Running a separate analysis for each cluster size group.  For each
analysis you'd use a different data filter, and each data filter would use
the data selection tab to select out the range of cluster sizes that apply
to that group (e.g., [Cluster size]>=1 AND [Cluster size]<=3).

One of these days, I'm planning to add a "Formula" facility to the data
sheets in Distance, where the values of each row in a field are specified as
a combination of values for that row in other fields.  Never seem to find
time for this sort of stuff...

Anyway, hope this helps,

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: Trapping web data entry
messages.body_plain:
Hi Humberto, list,

I've never collected trapping web data, but I can perhaps give some useful
advice about how to put it into Distance.

Each web is equivalent to a single point in a point transect design.  The
sample effort is the number of trapping events.  Each trapped animal is
equivalent to an observation in a point transect.  The distance of the trap
from the centre of the web is the distance to use for this "observation".

So, for example, say I had 1 stratum of area 100, containing 2 webs that I
used for two trapping events (say trap nights).  I trapped 3 animals in the
first (at distances 3, 5, 7) and 2 in the second (at distances 4, 5, 8) my
text file for data import might look like this:

area1 100 web1 2 3
area1 100 web1 2 5
area1 100 web1 2 7
area1 100 web1 2 4
area1 100 web1 2 5
area1 100 web1 2 8

Of course 2 webs is not enough to make reliable inferences about the stratum
density, nor is 6 observations enough to reliably fit a detection function,
but you get the idea.

Perhaps others who actually *have* analyzed such data in Distance can send
you some real projects, rather than just advice!

Lots more about trapping webs is in section 6.8 of the Introduction to
Distance Sampling book, and chapter 9 of the Advanced book discusses other
approaches such as trapping line transects.  You may also find the trapping
web simulation software WebSim written by Paul Lukacs useful in evaluating
the potential biases in your study
(http://www.cnr.colostate.edu/~plukacs/web.html)
If you get recapture information you may also want to consider using the
free software Density, by Murray Efford
(see http://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/services/software/density/ and
references on that page).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

messages.subject: evasive movement combined with blind strip under plane
messages.subject_clean: evasive movement combined with blind strip under plane
messages.body_plain:
Hi all (2)

=20

After such a speedy response to my first question today I am now
encouraged to ask another!

=20

Our aerial survey data of seaducks show evidence of evasive movement in
response to the plane (and the surveyors describe this too). This is
combined with a limitation in the data collection, since the observers
cannot see the sea surface beneath the plane to a distance of 44m either
side. The data are collected as cluster sizes in 4 bands which get wider
with distance from the plane.

=20

The problem is that an unknown proportion of the birds underneath the
plane are moving away from the flight path into the visible area,
leaving an equally unknown proportion behind. In addition there appears
to be evasive movement in the visible area too, with band B being higher
than band A.

I've looked through the archives for ways to tackle this kind of
problem, and none of the entries quite seem to match this problem.

=20

So far my approach has been to reduce the observation distances and
cut-points by 44m prior to analysis and assume that detection at 44m is
1 (although this obviously ignores the higher peak in B). To account for
the rising numbers between A and B I have fitted a haz-rate function
which splits the difference. However, I am concerned that I am risking
over-estimation of D, since the plane may have effectively squeezed all
the birds present near the transect (but un-observable) into a smaller
(but observable) area (i.e. the strip beneath the plane is 'empty' and
the surveyed area next to the plane has elevated numbers).

=20

I have been trying to come up with solutions to this based on the area
surveyed etc but have no solid answers yet.

=20

One I idea I had was if I could manually add 44m to the estimate of ESW
and then re-calculate D - would this only be valid under the assumption
that all birds have moved out of the 'blind' strip? (if so then this may
be a moderately acceptable assumption to make). If this is ok then I am
not sure how to re-calculate the variance estimators...=20

=20

Any help gratefully received.

=20

Mark

=20

=20

messages.subject: Number of transects required for survey
messages.subject_clean: Number of transects required for survey
messages.body_plain:
Could someone experienced with using Distance 5 software answer a question=20
for us?

What we would like to know is approximately how many transects to complete=20
to give us a reliable picture in Distance 5?  Even a percentage of the=20
study area to cover will help our planning.

Some background information follows:

In four weeks time (mid-October) we will undertake a coastal survey in=20
Albania searching for sea turtles (Caretta caretta) and Mediterranean Monk=20
Seals (Monachus monachus).  The project lasts about one month and will=20
operate from a small yacht.  The main stakeholders are the Albanian=20
Ministry of the Environment, Tirana University, Medasset (Greece), and=20
TurtlePoint, Napoli (Italy).

We will be looking at different aspects at various times: 1) a record of=20
occasional sightings of turtles and Monk Seals along the entire Albanian=20
coast,  2) pinpoint possible Monk Seal Refuges, such as caves or remote=20
coves, 3) detailed habitat surveys at Karaburuni and Patok =96 these will=20
include SCUBA diving surveys for turtles and their habitats.

Sea turtles are captured in fishing gear along much of the Albanian coast,=20
but particularly in Patok Lagoon.  The Albanian government wishes to=20
create a Marine Reserve at Karaburuni, and so our surveys will form part=20
of the inventory of species diversity.

Assuming that we find enough turtles we would like to use Distance 5 for=20
line transect data during our underwater surveys of turtle distribution=20
and abundance (Karaburuni and Patok).  We have a usable technique for=20
photo-identification of individual loggerheads (using facial scales and=20
carapace scutes), and we would be able to measure the distance from a=20
transect line underwater to a turtle (even if we had to wait until the=20
animals swam off).

We have read the paper by Evans and Hammond (2004) for cetacean=20
monitoring, and found many useful points for survey design.  Some=20
parameters that we have to contend with are: loggerhead turtles are mainly=20
solitary as juveniles and adults (some interactions do occur, mating being=20
the obvious one, but occasionally several animals may forage close to one=20
another on a particularly abundant food resource, such as crabs); turtles=20
are a migratory species throughout their lives; small juveniles tend to be=20
pelagic, larger turtles recruit into benthic habitats; they spend most=20
(90%) of their time submerged; they may show short-term fidelity to a=20
particular sea area for some weeks; much of their life cycle remains=20
unstudied.  For diving sites the visibility may vary from day to day.

Thanks in advance,=20

Michael White, Marine Zoologist, Centro Recupero Tartarughe Marine, 92010=20
Lampedusa (AG), Italia.=20

--

messages.subject: Re: Number of transects required for survey
messages.subject_clean: Number of transects required for survey
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vassilis, (cc list)

You should read chapter 7 of Introduction to Distance Sampling, which covers
survey design and field methods.  There are some formulae in section 7.2.2
that can suggest a total transect length, given some pilot data or some
assumptions.  These don't help you with number of transects however.  As it
says in Section 7.2.1, you want a minimum of 10-20 transects (that is per
stratum).  More than 20 gives you an even better picture of the true level of
spatial variation in density.  If this variation is high, you need to think
about stratification to reduce variance.

There is also a whole chapter in the Advanced Distance Sampling book on
automated survey design and using the GIS facilities in Distance (chapter 7).

Hope this helps!

 - len

--

messages.subject: Treatment of extraordinary groups
messages.body_plain:
Hello

=20

I have recently completed an aerial whale survey where I can see we will =
have a problem with the analysis. For fin and humpback whales, most =
groups were between 1 and 5 animals. However there were 6 groups of >50 =
animals, and 2 of these were mixed groups with large numbers of both =
species.

=20

These large groups have of course very different sighting =
characteristics from "normal" groups. However there are only 6 of them =
so it will not be possible to derive a separate pdf for them. If they =
are just blended with the other sightings, the estimation of mean group =
size will be very imprecise for those blocks in which they occur.

=20

I am wondering if it might be advisable to treat these large groups =
separately in some way, perhaps by analyzing just the large sightings as =
a strip survey, with some strip width that seems reasonable for them. =
They can be seen from quite far away. The smaller groups would be =
analyzed as a normal line transect or cue counting survey in DISTANCE.

=20

I would appreciate any other ideas for the treatment of these =
extraordinary sightings, and I will of course provide a summary of any =
suggestions received back to the group.

=20

Thanks in advance,

=20

Daniel Pike

Scientific Secretary

messages.subject: Re: map import
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 15 Sep 2005 10:34:17 -0700, Shana Rapoport wrote:

> >Hello.  I am new to Distance and am having difficulty importing a GIS map.
> >I have the shapefile but do not have any ESRI software to do the necessary
> >editing for the import to Distance.  Does anyone know of a program that will
> >enable me to open and edit the shapefile?

> >Thank you,
> >Shana

In case anyone else is interested in this, below is the reply I sent to Shana
last week.  Also, I've just added the ability in Distance to cut and paste the
coordinates of a shape to and from text and spreadsheet files - which should
make it easier for those without a GIS to import geographic data into
Distance.  This facility will be in the next release of Distance.

 - Len

-------------------------------------------------------------------
From: "Distance Development" <dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>
To: "Shana Rapoport" <sbrap...@hotmail.com>
Date: Thu, 22 Sep 2005 17:28:28 +0100

Hi Shana,

I Googled around a bit, and came up with
http://www.digitalgrove.net/fgis.htm
which might work for you.  I haven't tried it, so please let me (and the list)
know if it works.  If it doesn't work, let me know and I'll Google round a bit
more -- or perhaps you can try the same approach!  Whatever you find out, I'd
be very grateful if you could post a summary of your findings to the list, to
help future people who have a similar question.  Thanks!

 - Len Thomas
